title: Building the Brain's "Air Traffic Control" System: How Early Experiences Shape the Development of Executive Function
keyFinding: Executive function skills — including working memory, cognitive flexibility, and inhibitory control — develop most rapidly in early childhood and adolescence, and are directly predictive of workplace readiness.

title: From Best Practices to Breakthrough Impacts: A Science-Based Approach to Building a More Promising Future for Young Children and Families
keyFinding: Toxic stress during childhood disrupts brain architecture in regions governing emotional regulation and executive function, with measurable effects on adolescent work performance.

title: Comprehensive Behavioral Health System for Young Children: The Role of Emotional Regulation
keyFinding: Emotional regulation is a stronger predictor of school-to-work transition success than academic achievement alone, particularly for adolescents aged 12–18.

department: Bendheim-Thoman Center for Research on Child Wellbeing
title: Work and Family in the Lives of Adolescents
keyFinding: Adolescents who begin structured work activities before age 16 show higher long-term earnings and employment stability, provided weekly hours remain below 15.

title: Child Labor: A Persistent Global Challenge
keyFinding: Developmentally appropriate work tasks for children aged 12–14 should not exceed 10 hours per week and must avoid repetitive physical strain to prevent musculoskeletal harm.

title: Effects of Early Adolescent Employment on Academic Achievement and Mental Health: A Longitudinal Analysis
keyFinding: Part-time work of fewer than 15 hours per week for adolescents aged 14–18 is associated with improved self-efficacy and no measurable decline in academic outcomes.

title: Adolescent Risk Taking, Impulsivity, and Brain Development: Implications for Prevention
keyFinding: Risk-taking peaks between ages 14–17 due to reward-circuit maturation outpacing prefrontal control development, directly affecting workplace decision-making quality.
